lines.note: Hoejini denotes dying while barking or howling. The enlarged scan preserves weak traces of n before the final i; the supplied NINJAL index corroborates Foyejini after independent inspection. The OCR split Foyeji. i. is rejected, although the n remains damaged. The independent second pass establishes vyuãdo, with a worn u rather than OCR i. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho v202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); this transcription and its revisions are independently scan-based.
The figurative extension describes dying while weeping and speaking. The final falã- continues as falando across the physical line break; the tilde and terminal hyphen are visible.
Completes falando baixamente, speaking in a low or subdued manner. This short Portuguese continuation belongs to the preceding figurative sense of hoeji.
Hoemawari, hoemawaru, hoemawatta means going around barking. The principal parts fit a four-grade verb; la- begins Portuguese ladrando, completed below.
Completes ladrando and thus the description of going around barking. No independent headword or additional sense begins on this short row.
Hooyen denotes square and round shapes. The headword visibly contains y, not OCR punctuation; redõda abbreviates redonda with a tilde over o. Fǒ- begins the compound example below.
The divided example is hooyen chootan, square/round and long/short. The Portuguese lists the same contrasts; compri- begins comprido on the following row.
Completes comprido and adds curto, long and short. This closes the fourfold contrast introduced by hooyen chootan.
A separate hooyen entry is paraphrased as koobashii sono, a fragrant garden. The scan supplies a real word space in Iardim de; this is not the preceding geometrical sense.
Fragrant roses complete the Portuguese garden definition. The shared headword spelling does not merge this entry with the preceding square-and-round sense.

Hoeki is replenishment or restoration, explained by oginoi and masu, supplying and increasing. The scan supports maſu, not OCR raſu. Portuguese restaurar is divided after reſ without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: taurar algũa couſa falta, ou diminuida. Vſaſe

lines.note: Completes restaurar: restoring something deficient or diminished. Vſaſe begins the usage qualification continued below; historical spelling and the tilde carrier in algũa are retained.

runs.text: particularmente em mezinhas que confortão, ou

lines.note: The term is particularly applied to strengthening remedies. The printed confortão, supported by the visible t, replaces OCR conforião; this records the dictionary's historical explanation, not a modern treatment claim.
The remedies give strength and vigour. Ki no fusoku wo begins an example about a deficiency of vital energy, with uo functioning as the object particle.
Hoeki suru completes the Japanese example of replenishing the deficiency. The Portuguese reads Refazer, with f rather than long s, and starts coração across the line boundary.

runs.text: ção, ou falta de eſpiritos vitaes.

lines.note: Completes coração and relates the replenishment to a lack of vital spirits. The wording belongs to the source's historical account of vitality, without imposing modern physiological equivalence.
Hoezura is equated with nakizura, a crying face. The doubled zz and the alternative marker l are retained; the Portuguese noun phrase continues onto the next line.

runs.text: de quem chora. Vſa ſe com gente baxa.

lines.note: The face is that of someone crying. The usage qualification says the expression is used with low-status people; this is the dictionary's social register judgment, not the reviewer's description.
Hooyoo is explained by awa and kage, foam and shadow. The Portuguese confirms both images; ſõ- starts the abbreviated spelling of sombra on the next row.

runs.text: bra. i, Couſa que logo ſe acaba, & perece.

lines.note: Completes sombra and explains the metaphor as something that soon ends and perishes. This is a transience gloss, not another independent headword.

Hoyoo means sustaining or nourishing, explained by tamochi and yashinoo. The example begins Ichi-, not OCR chi-; the following mei makes ichimei, one's life. Soſtentar replaces the garbled OCR Seſtentas.
Ichi- plus mei forms ichimei wo hoyoo suru, sustaining life. The Portuguese directly confirms this reading; the visible short-s/t form in Sostentar is not harmonized with the preceding line.

runs.text: Lugar onde ſe prèga da ley,

lines.note: Hooza is nori no za, a place for preaching the religious law. The source's ley has a religious referent here, as the following ceremonial qualification confirms.
The location also serves for ceremonies. Hooza wo begins an example in which this ritual or preaching place is decorated.
Kazaru completes hooza wo kazaru, adorning the place or building. The short Japanese verb belongs to the preceding example rather than a new entry.
Hoozai is paraphrased as tsumi no mukui, recompense for sin. The Portuguese reads Satiſfação, with the distinct ſ/f sequence, and divides peccado after pec-.
Completes peccado and introduces hoozai no tsukunoi wo suru, making satisfaction or atonement. The opening cado is physical text on this row and must not be omitted.
The translation is making satisfaction for sins. The scan shows pollos, including the doubled l, rather than the OCR's reduced plos; the historical contraction is retained.

runs.text: Pee da fruita como de melão, peras,

lines.note: Hozo is the stalk or attachment of fruit, exemplified by melon and pears. The printed Portuguese is Pee, with two e letters and no supplied accent.
Hashira no hozo names a column's tenon. The repeated word is fozo, not OCR fezo; the Portuguese starts its description as the narrowed projecting end.

runs.text: da colũna pera encaxar em outro pao.

lines.note: The narrowed end of the column fits into another piece of wood, completing the tenon definition. The abbreviation colũna and historical encaxar are retained.
Hoozoo is takara kura, a storehouse or treasury. Gudão is the printed warehouse term; fa- begins fato, goods or belongings, on the next row.

runs.text: to. ¶ Item, No Ximo bolſa que ſe traz

lines.note: Completes fato, then gives a regional sense: in Ximo the word denotes a pouch carried on the belt. Ximo is a Japanese regional name embedded in Portuguese and is separately eligible for typeface review.

runs.text: dependurada no cinto. No Cami ſe diz,

lines.note: The pouch hangs from the belt. The Portuguese then supplies the Cami-region names, beginning the divided fiuchibucuro; Cami and the following named forms occur within this Portuguese explanation.
Completes fiuchibucuro and gives kinchaku as an alternative regional designation. These named alternatives finish the preceding Portuguese sentence, rather than forming a new Japanese entry.
Hoozon is respectful consideration, with koobashuu zonzuru as its Japanese explanation. Portuguese pe- begins pejo, reserve or embarrassment, completed below. The caron in Fǒzon is retained.

Completes the definition as reserve in speaking. The example begins hoozon mo noo, without such reserve. Two following physical rows have no stable IDs in the supplied baseline; their readings and proposed positions are reported in structural_changes rather than inserted by renumbering.

Completes Fǒzonmonǒ monouo yǔ: speaking freely without respectful reserve. The Portuguese says without embarrassment. Initial m is damaged and n-like; monouo is the adopted contextual reading, not a securely preserved individual glyph.

runs.text: reſpeito da peſoa de que ſe falla. ¶

lines.note: Completes the absence of respect for the person spoken about. Fǒzon begins the contrasting example continued by uo voqu on the following physical line.

This completes Fǒzon uo voqu, having or maintaining such respectful reserve. Its Fǒzon is on the second unrepresented row above; this line must not be directly joined to Fǒzonmonǒ on c1-l037. The structural omission remains pending.
Hozoochi or hozoochi no uri describes a melon whose stalk separates at ripeness. The second form repeats fozo-, not OCR fizo-; the Portuguese ripeness qualification continues below.

runs.text: maduro q̃ per ſi da o pee. ¶ Item, Per-

lines.note: The ripe melon releases its stalk by itself. The printed q̃ remains abbreviated and has a word space before per; Per- introduces the figurative extension on the next row.

runs.text: met. Conſentir hum de ſua liure vontade ſem

lines.note: The figurative meaning is consenting of one's own free will. The Portuguese emphasizes voluntary action and continues with the absence of force.

Completes the consent gloss, without coercion. The example is associated with fozouochi above, but the second rounded letter in the printed Fozoucchiga is abraded; the provisional OCR form is retained pending graphic adjudication.
Shita and serareta finish the example, with ordinary and respectful alternatives. Their relation to the preceding voluntary-consent expression is preserved despite the damaged spelling on c1-l042.
Hozue is a flowering branch or sprig of roses. The scan reads Fozuye, not Fizuye. The final P. is the upright poetry-use label, outside the italic Portuguese definition.

Hozuna denotes the ship's rigging ropes. The headword's final n, corroborated lexically by the supplied NINJAL index after visual reading, replaces OCR u; the Portuguese rigging term is read enxarcias, with worn middle letters requiring caution.
Hoozuki is identified simply as an herb bearing this name. The short gloss does not itself justify adding a modern botanical species identification.

runs.text: O encoſtar o roſto na mão. ¶

lines.note: Hoozue means resting the face on the hand. The repeated example is divided Fôz- / zuyeuo; the line-end mark is a hyphen, not the OCR period.

Completes hoozue wo tsuku, supporting the face on one's hand. The Portuguese has Encoſtar, including t. The narrow printed aface spacing is retained rather than regularized to the modern word division.

Fu is shirushi, a sign or seal. The enlarged initial is F, not OCR L. Mutra is genuine historical Portuguese: the Caldas Aulete original entry defines a seal or signet (https://www.aulete.com.br/mutra); it is not an OCR corruption of mostra.
Fu wo tsukuru or nasu means making or applying a mark. Por sinal begins the Portuguese rendering, continued by mutrar below; the divided Fu- belongs to this example.

Completes the alternative Portuguese verb for applying a seal or mark. The Caldas Aulete original mutrar entry independently confirms this historical verb (https://www.aulete.com.br/mutrar); the printed r must not be replaced with OCR t.
Fuu denotes custom or conduct; fuu no yoi hito is a person of good habits. The scan shows a long-u mark in both occurrences, not OCR Fa or Fino. The accent's downward opening supports ǔ.
Completes homem de bons costumes, the person of good conduct in the Japanese example. This is distinct from the luck or fortune sense beginning below.
Fu here means luck or fortune. Fu no yoi begins the favourable alternative, with l introducing warui on the next row.
Warui hito completes the alternative 'person of bad fortune'. The Portuguese contrasts a fortunate person with an unfortunate one, dividing afortunado at afor-.
Completes afortunado after the preceding mal. No full stop is supplied merely to regularize the entry's ending; the printed short continuation is retained.

runs.text: Bolinhos pequenos feitos de ſemeas, ou fa-

lines.note: Fu is described as small wheat-derived cakes. The Portuguese reads ſemeas, bran or coarse milling material, rather than OCR ſeneas; fa- begins the alternative farelos.
Completes farelos de trigo, wheat bran. This closes the source's description of the food without replacing it with a modern ingredient formula.

Fu is the fu of gozoo roppu, the traditional five-and-six classification of internal organs. The Portuguese defines any one of the six; this is the source's anatomical terminology rather than a modern organ list.

runs.text: quer das ſeis que ha nas entranhas, ou partes

lines.note: Completes qualquer and specifies one of the six parts located in the viscera. The phrase partes interiores continues below.
Interiores completes the description of internal parts. It remains a separate physical continuation of the fu anatomical entry.
Fuba is explained by soe uma, an accompanying horse. The Portuguese describes a horse led alongside or at the hand; it is not a different entry for an ordinary riding horse.
Fubako is fumi no hako, a small box for letters. The Portuguese verb begins le- and continues with uão on the following line.
Completes leuão as cartas, the letters being carried in the box. The damaged initial is u rather than OCR p; the continuation is not an independent noun.
Fuben is deficiency or want, explained by tarawazu, not being sufficient. The Portuguese applies this lack to more than one domain, specified below.
The deficiency may concern knowledge, wealth, or possessions. This completes the broad lack-or-insufficiency sense and prepares the following terms for a poor person.
Fubenjin and fubensha are alternative designations for a poor person. The Portuguese Pobre supplies the shared gloss; the alternatives remain on one physical line.
Fubenna repeats the poverty sense through Idem. The scan does not support the OCR's additional i in Fubennia; the following entry uses the same adjectival form in another sense.
Fubenna is now explained as ben no kanawanu hito, someone unable to speak eloquently. The apparent extra i in OCR Fuibenna comes from damaged type, not a separate syllable.

runs.text: de pouca eloquencia, & que ſe não ſabe bem

lines.note: The Portuguese describes little eloquence and difficulty expressing oneself well. Its final bem modifies explicar on the following row.
Completes the ineloquence gloss, then gives fubenna chie, deficient understanding or knowledge. The Portuguese saber is divided after ſa-.
Completes saber and adds falto, deficient. This continuation qualifies the knowledge example rather than supplying a new headword.
The adverbial fubenni and nominal fubensa follow the adjective. Both are Japanese derivative forms, not words embedded in a Portuguese sentence, so they are not typeface-term candidates.
Fubi appears in the letter formula kyookyoo fubi and is explained by sonawarazu, not being complete. The alternative explanatory paraphrase continues on the next row; Vt is italic in the scan.
Kuwashuu moosanu means not stating the matter in detail. The Portuguese renders this as not writing more fully, making the epistolary function of fubi clear.

runs.text: ou mais miudamente. Palaura de cartas falan-

lines.note: The writer does not give further detail. The gloss explicitly calls this an expression used in letters and divides falando at falan-.
Completes falando com respeito, speaking respectfully. This closes the register qualification for the letter-ending formula.
Fubin is something pitiful or distressing, paraphrased by itawashii koto. The visible headword vowel is i, not OCR Fuban; com- begins compaixão.
Completes compaixão and introduces fubin shigokuna koto ja, a matter deserving the utmost pity. The Portuguese copula begins the translation on this row.
The example is translated as a matter of great compassion and misery. Fu begins fubinni on the next row without adding a hyphen not established in the print.
Fu plus binni yields fubinni omoo, feeling compassion for someone. The Portuguese directly confirms this compassionate sense rather than the different ability-related entry below.
A separate fubin means lacking quickness or ability, explained by tokarazu and don na koto. The scan reads Fubin, not Fibin; rude- begins rudeza.
Completes rudeza and gives pouca habilidade, little ability. Waga mi fubin begins a self-deprecating example; the headword is repeated as fubin rather than OCR fibin.

Nari to iyedomo completes the concessive expression, although I am lacking in ability. The faded y in iyedomo is supported by its descender and the Japanese construction; OCR's separated i edomo is rejected.
Completes the Portuguese concession: although not so capable and quick, nevertheless. The initial is lowercase h in habil, not OCR capital B; historical toda via remains separated.

Fuubin is kaze no tayori, an opportunity for conveying a message. The Portuguese describes an available carrier. The worn Japanese letters support Cajeno tayori, not OCR Cajeto tayeni, and the gloss reads Portador.
Completes offerece, the carrier who presents himself or becomes available. This brief continuation closes the message-opportunity sense of fuubin.
Fubinna qualifies something miserable or pitiable. The headword contains b, not OCR h; Latin vel introduces the alternative application to a person on the next row.
The adjective can describe a pitiable person who arouses compassion. The scan supports this coherent Portuguese clause in place of the heavily garbled OCR; the printed single-ſ peſoa is retained.
Fubinni is the corresponding adverbial form, compassionately or with pity. The crop shows two consecutive n letters, not the OCR's additional i syllable in Fubinini.

Fubinsa is the corresponding abstract noun, pitiableness or compassion. The initial F replaces OCR T. A separate catchword is also visible at the right edge, but remains in its existing furniture record.
